rationale.problem: The render sandbox captures a fixed viewport, while the locked upstream authoring reference mandates a 1920x1080 stage. A composition that followed the reference rendered as the empty top-left corner of its own stage: 180 byte-identical frames encoded into a valid MP4 that was a still image. Neither the authoring gates nor the render sandbox could observe the disagreement, because neither knew the other's number.
rationale.resolution: The capture viewport is one declared value read by every side. The authoring gate rejects any composition whose declared stage differs from it, so the mismatch fails before a browser is launched rather than after an MP4 exists.
rationale.changing: Raising the canvas means changing this file and the sandbox spec together; the still-frame gate in the render job is the backstop that keeps a future mismatch loud.
rationale.scale: Sharper output is bought with deviceScaleFactor, not with a larger stage. Every type and spacing rule in composition_template is written for a 640x360 stage — 42px headlines, 40px padding — so enlarging the stage would leave them adrift in a bigger frame rather than filling it, and would require rewriting the whole scale. A higher device pixel ratio re-rasterises text and vector art at the target resolution with no layout rule touched. outputWidth/outputHeight are width/height times this factor and are what a captured PNG actually measures; the composition still declares width/height, which is what the authoring gate compares against. Measured 2026-07-27 on the packaged Chromium with a real catalog part: the per-frame cost of factor 2 sits inside the run-to-run noise of factor 1, so this is close to free. Raising it again (3 gives 1920x1080) needs the same measurement repeated, because cost is not linear in pixels.

film.$comment: What the finished file is, as opposed to what any one render was. Route A captures each shot on the stage its part declares — 1920x1080 for 105 of the catalog, 1080x1920 for three, 1440x2560 for one, 640x360 at factor 2 for the built-in template — and a delivered film is one size throughout. So every segment is brought onto this canvas as it is encoded, and the joined result is measured against it afterwards. Measured 2026-07-28 with the packaged ffmpeg: joining a 1920x1080 segment to a 1080x1920 one through the concat demuxer with `-c copy` exits 0 and reports 279 frames and 9.300000 seconds, both exactly the sums, while the second half is portrait content inside a container claiming landscape. Every cheap check passes and the file is broken, which is why nothing here treats an exit code or a frame count as evidence that a join worked.
film.framingsRationale: The two framings are the ones motion-one-sentence-brief.v1.json offers; a third would be added in both files or the App would accept a brief it cannot deliver. The sizes are the stage 105 of the 134 parts already declare, so the common case is a scale of 1:1 and the pad is empty.
film.fitRationale: A segment is scaled to fit and the remainder padded, never stretched: the part was laid out for the stage it declares, and stretching it is a design change nobody asked for. `setsar=1` is required rather than tidy — without it a padded stream carries the source's sample aspect ratio and a player stretches the result back.

requestedCanvas.$comment: What one render may ask its viewport to be. The template canvas above is still a fixed pair — `composition_template` writes its whole type scale for 640x360 and the authoring gate compares against it. A catalog part is a different thing: an independent composition that declares its own stage, and rendering it on the template's stage captures the top-left corner of it. Measured on the frozen catalog: 105 parts declare 1920x1080, three declare 1080x1920 portrait and one 1440x2560, so the viewport has to travel with the request. The bounds are what keeps that from becoming an open dial: a render that asks for something outside them is refused before a browser starts.
requestedCanvas.pixelsRationale: 1920x1080 at factor 1, and 640x360 at factor 2, both sit inside this. It is the product of output pixels, because that is what a captured PNG costs and what the per-frame budget in motion-render-sandbox-budget.v1.json is written against. Raising it needs the same measurement the deviceScaleFactor rationale above demands, for the same reason: cost is not linear in pixels.
